# My grooming van almost caught fire. Here’s what I wish I’d checked.

Last Wednesday, October 28, at about 2:15 in the afternoon, I was in a client’s driveway in Bedford, drying a damp Bernese mountain dog named Moose.

The dryer was on high. Normal appointment, normal afternoon. Then I smelled hot plastic.

At first I thought it was the dryer motor. That was the thing running in my hand, so that was where my brain went. Then I saw smoke coming out of the bench seat where the batteries live.

I shut off the battery switch and got Moose out through the side door, still damp. Moose was honestly thrilled by this unexpected change of plans.

I used a bit of the fire extinguisher. I still don’t know whether I needed to. What I do know is that the positive cable connection was blackened and about three centimetres of the cable jacket had melted back.

Everyone is okay. Moose is okay. Nobody was hurt.

His mum brought me a coffee and sat with me on her front steps while I shook.

I’m writing this because a lot of the people who read this blog are other groomers. One of them, Tasha, is about to put down a deposit with the same person who built my van. I want her—and anyone else spending their savings on a mobile setup—to have more useful information than “oh my God, be careful.”

I also need to say this right at the beginning: **I’m not an electrician. This is what happened in my van, what the electrician found afterward, and what I now know to ask about. It is not a guide to wiring or repairing your own electrical system.**

## The setup I trusted

I’m a mobile dog groomer in Halifax. My van is my workplace and my whole income.

The conversion was built by Darren at Coastline Van Fitouts in spring 2025. The electrical setup included a 3,000-watt inverter and two 200Ah lithium batteries in a 12-volt system.

I’m naming the builder because people who read this are making decisions about their own builds. I’m not trying to turn this into a pile-on. I’ve sent Darren three texts and an email, and as I write this, I haven’t had a response. I don’t have his explanation to include.

The van looked tidy when I got it. The wiring wasn’t hanging everywhere. The battery setup was tucked away under a bench. It looked like something someone who knew what they were doing had built.

That was enough for me at the time.

It turns out I didn’t know what I needed to be looking at. I could judge whether the cupboards were finished properly and whether the grooming layout worked. I couldn’t judge the cable supplying the inverter or the quality of a connection hidden under heat-shrink.

I trusted the build because it looked tidy.

**Tidy is not the same as right.**

## What Priya found

Afterward, Priya from Sackville Marine Electric inspected the system.

The cable between the battery and inverter was **4 AWG**. Priya told me that for my 3,000-watt, 12-volt inverter installation, it should have been **2/0 AWG**.

For anyone whose electrical knowledge is roughly where mine was: those are very different cable sizes. And yes, the naming system is confusing. “2/0,” also written “00,” is much bigger than 4 AWG. It is not the same as 2 AWG.

That does **not** mean everyone should read this, buy some 2/0 cable and consider their van sorted. The right cable depends on the inverter manufacturer’s requirements, the length of the cable run, the insulation rating, how it’s routed and other installation details. Priya’s recommendation was for my setup.

She also found a problem with the lug on the positive connection. The lug is the metal terminal attached to the end of the cable.

According to Priya, the crimp appeared to have been made with something like pliers or a hammer rather than the appropriate crimping tool. I didn’t watch that connection being made, so I can’t tell you exactly what was used. I can tell you what she showed me afterward: a connection she identified as improperly crimped, with heat damage around it.

Heat-shrink had covered the connection. From the outside, it hadn’t looked like an obvious problem to me.

There was also a **300-amp ANL fuse**, mounted roughly **90 centimetres from the battery**. Priya told me the protection should have been much closer—around 18 centimetres for the arrangement she was discussing.

Those were the main findings I wrote down. The cable size, the connection and the fuse arrangement all needed attention.

## Why a dog dryer means so much current on the battery side

This is the bit I wanted explained properly, because “3,000-watt inverter” sounded comfortably bigger than my dryer.

My dryer draws around **1,800 to 2,000 watts**. There’s also a water heater that sometimes runs. I don’t have a measurement showing exactly what everything was drawing at the moment this happened, or confirmation that the heater was on.

The simple calculation is:

**Watts ÷ volts = amps.**

At 12 volts:

- 1,800 watts ÷ 12 volts = **150 amps**
- 2,000 watts ÷ 12 volts = **about 167 amps**
- 3,000 watts ÷ 12 volts = **250 amps**

Those are simplified figures, before allowing for inverter losses. The inverter uses some energy itself while converting battery power to the power my equipment needs, so at a given battery voltage, its input current is higher than the simple calculation suggests.

Battery voltage also changes in use. That means these aren’t exact readings from my van. They explain the scale of what the battery cable has to carry.

The dryer alone can mean well over a hundred amps on the 12-volt side. Additional loads increase that demand.

Also, the inverter’s 3,000-watt rating doesn’t mean it constantly draws 3,000 watts. What’s plugged in and running matters. But the installation still has to be designed properly for its intended loads and equipment ratings.

Two big batteries do not make an undersized cable safe. Having enough stored energy to run the dryer is a different question from whether the wiring can safely deliver that energy.

That distinction had never really landed for me before.

## How a bad connection gets hot

Priya explained that a poor connection can create resistance right where the current has to pass through it.

At the sort of current an inverter can draw, even a small amount of extra resistance can create serious heat in one spot. You don’t need the whole cable run to look terrible for one connection to become dangerous.

There’s a formula for this—heat generated through resistance goes up with the square of the current—but my practical takeaway is simpler: **a high-current connection has to be properly made, not just attached firmly enough that it stays on.**

A lug can be covered neatly in heat-shrink and still have a bad crimp underneath. The covering doesn’t prove the electrical connection is good.

In my van, the blackened lug and melted insulation were at that connection. Priya identified the poor crimp and undersized cable as serious problems. I’m not going to pretend I can separate their exact contributions from my notes or diagnose every part of the failure myself.

What I saw was smoke coming from the battery compartment while I was working. What she found afterward was not a system she considered acceptable to put back into service.

## “But didn’t you have a fuse?”

Yes. That was one of my questions too.

There was a 300A ANL fuse. I had assumed that if something electrical became dangerous, the fuse would blow.

It is not that simple.

A fuse responds to current according to its rating and how long that current flows. **It is not a temperature sensor at every cable connection.** A poor connection can get dangerously hot while the current remains below what would make the fuse open promptly.

The fuse also has to be coordinated with the wiring and the equipment. Putting a large fuse in a system doesn’t automatically make it safer. The cable it is protecting has to be suitable for the protection provided.

Then there’s location.

The length of positive cable between the battery and the fuse is not protected by that fuse against a short to the vehicle body. That’s why having the fuse close to the source matters, and why Priya flagged the roughly 90-centimetre distance in my van.

The roughly 18-centimetre figure she mentioned is not a universal DIY rule I’m qualified to apply to every vehicle. Exact requirements and permitted arrangements depend on the installation and relevant guidance. “Near the battery” is something I now want an electrician to explain and verify, not something I’ll judge from across the van.

My repair quote includes a **Class T fuse**. One reason fuse type matters, especially with lithium batteries, is its ability to safely interrupt the very high current a battery system may deliver during a short circuit.

The amp rating is only part of that decision.

Please don’t take this as an instruction to swap an ANL fuse for a Class T fuse yourself. The fuse, holder, cables, battery system and inverter need to work together as a properly designed installation.

## What the photos showed—and what they didn’t

Priya pulled up my damage photos beside thermal-camera images of her own van running a similar kind of load.

The difference was wild. Mine showed a blackened connection and melted insulation. Her thermal images showed very little warming in the setup she was demonstrating.

That helped me understand why she was concerned. This wasn’t something I should accept as normal just because a dryer uses a lot of power.

But it wasn’t a controlled comparison. A damage photo isn’t a temperature reading, and another van’s temperatures don’t establish a safe limit for mine. Cable lengths, installation details, ambient temperature and how long equipment has been running can all affect what you see.

For me, it made the explanation easier to understand. It wasn’t a substitute for her inspection.

## The £—sorry, $40 thermometer I wish I’d understood earlier

I bought an infrared thermometer at Canadian Tire for about **$40**.

I think it can be a useful thing to own, provided you understand what it cannot do. It reads surface temperatures. It cannot see through heat-shrink, into a connection or through a closed battery box. Shiny metal can give misleading readings.

A reassuring number does not certify that your wiring is safe.

I’m going to ask Priya to show me which accessible surfaces I can check safely after the repairs, what normal looks like for my van, and what changes mean I should stop using it and call her.

I am **not** recommending that anyone open up a live battery compartment and run the dryer to see what gets hot. If there’s already a hot-plastic smell, discoloration, melting or smoke, don’t run another test.

The thermometer is an extra observation tool. It isn’t permission to keep working around a suspected fault.

## A power-off checklist for other groomers

This is the checklist I wish I’d had, with a very important limit:

**Switching the inverter off does not make the batteries or every cable dead. Neither does turning off one battery switch necessarily isolate every source.**

Shore power, solar, charging equipment and the batteries themselves can leave parts of a system energised. Follow your system’s documented shutdown instructions. If you don’t have those instructions, ask a qualified professional to establish them.

This is a **look-and-document checklist**, not a repair checklist. Only look at things you can access safely without removing electrical covers, reaching near terminals or disturbing wiring.

### 1. Gather the paperwork

Find the inverter model and manual, battery details, wiring diagram, fuse specifications and any commissioning or inspection records you were given.

Don’t have them? Write that down as the first thing to request.

### 2. Record visible cable markings

If the main cable’s size is printed somewhere you can read safely, photograph it.

Don’t cut insulation or peel back heat-shrink to investigate. Don’t assume an unmarked cable is fine—or wrong—based on how thick it looks from the outside.

Ask an electrician to check the cable specification against the actual installation.

### 3. Look for visible damage

Without touching or moving anything, look for:

- Melted, discoloured or cracked insulation.
- Blackening around connections.
- Cable rubbing against metal edges.
- Exposed copper.
- Loose-looking or unsupported wiring.
- Water leaks or dampness near electrical equipment.

Any heat damage needs professional attention before the system is used again.

### 4. Note the fuse information you can see

Record visible labels and the approximate location. Don’t remove a fuse or its protective cover to get a better look.

Ask your electrician whether its rating, type, interrupting capacity and location are appropriate—not simply whether a fuse exists.

### 5. Check the space around the equipment

Are towels, bottles or other supplies blocking ventilation openings? Could stored equipment slide into wiring? Is the battery area being used as extra storage?

Only move ordinary stored items if doing so won’t bring you near exposed electrical parts or disturb the installation.

### 6. Find the shutdown instructions

Do you know where the emergency controls are? Can you reach them quickly? Do you understand what each one actually disconnects?

Find that out before you’re standing there smelling plastic with a dog on the table.

### 7. Check your alarm and extinguisher arrangements

I had no smoke alarm in the rear grooming area—only the one in the cab.

I’m getting advice on suitable detection and placement for the back, including the effects of grooming dust, moisture and airflow. Check existing alarms according to their instructions, and have your extinguisher’s suitability, condition and accessibility checked too.

### 8. Book an inspection if anything is uncertain

A visual check can flag a problem. It cannot clear a system as safe.

Ask someone qualified and experienced with mobile inverter and lithium-battery installations to inspect it. Tell them what equipment you actually use together, not just what appliances are installed.

## Tasha: before you pay that deposit

This bit is specifically for Tasha, but please borrow it.

Before paying a builder, ask for the electrical specifications **in writing**:

- What inverter and battery models are being fitted?
- What loads is the system designed to run simultaneously?
- What size are the main battery cables, and how was that size selected?
- What fuse type and rating will be used, and where will it go?
- How will cables be protected from rubbing, movement and moisture?
- Who will make and inspect the high-current connections?
- What standards and manufacturer instructions will the installation follow?
- Will you receive a wiring diagram, shutdown instructions and test records?
- Can an independent electrician inspect it before handover?

You don’t need to understand every answer yourself. You can take the specifications to someone who does.

A builder saying “we always do it this way” wouldn’t be enough for me now. Neither would photographs of a neat finished conversion.

I wish I’d paid for an independent electrical inspection before I started taking dogs into mine.

## If you smell burning, the appointment is over

My first thought was that the dryer motor was hot. I didn’t immediately understand where the smell was coming from.

If something like this happens, stop working. Get yourself, the animal and anyone else out. If you can operate an emergency disconnect safely, without approaching smoke or fire, do so—but don’t delay getting out.

For smoke or suspected fire, get clear and call 911. Don’t go back inside to investigate.

I used my extinguisher during the incident. That isn’t advice to stay and fight a fire. Extinguishers have limits, and batteries introduce hazards I’m not qualified to assess. A van is replaceable. You and the dog aren’t.

## Where things stand now

The repair quote is **$4,200**. It includes rewiring the main runs, a new fuse block and a Class T fuse.

Parts are on order. I’ve been told **at least three weeks** off the road.

So far, I’ve cancelled **31 appointments**.

Insurance is still a maybe. The adjuster is due Thursday, and until I have a decision, I don’t know what will be covered.

I’m scared. I’m relieved everyone is fine, obviously, but I’m also staring at a van I can’t work in and thinking about rent being due on the first. Those feelings are all happening at once.

Thank you to the clients who’ve been kind about cancellations. And thank you to Moose’s mum for the coffee and for sitting with me when I couldn’t stop shaking.

I’ll post another update when the repairs are finished and the van is back. I’ll share what was changed and what Priya wants me checking going forward.

For now, please get the specifications, ask the awkward questions and have someone qualified look at your setup. I wish I’d done it before there was smoke.
